# State of the Art in Missingness-Aware Learning {#sec-background}

* Multivariate Imputation by Chained Equations and its variants
* Ensemble methods - HyperImpute, RF-GAP
* Modern deep learning-based / generative supervised imputation methods - GAIN, MIRACLE, ReMasker, etc.
* Imputation in time-series: LOCF, CSDI, DISK, etc.
* kNN imputation: History and controversies (IQ and the Wealth of Nations, 2005)
* (Morvan and Varoquaux, 2025) - why better imputation doesn't necessarily imply better downstream task performance.
* Models for joint imputation-downstream task: NeuMiss, GRAPE, etc. (Relate to [Chapter -@sec-knnTheory])
* Models that perform downstream tasks without imputation - FLDA (Relate to [Chapter -@sec-mudra])
* Models that perform imputation in more complex structures, eg. graphs (Relate to [Chapter -@sec-fuse])

## Iterative Imputation

One of the earliest major advancements in multivariate imputation was by @mice, called `MICE`. `MICE` is a general approach that starts off from a naive imputation, and then iteratively fits a univariate regression model on each feature to impute the missing feature values. It is computationally efficient, highly adaptable as it can be used with any regression model. It can also specify different regression models for each features, and this can be used for all types of tabular data, be it numeric, categorical, or mixed. Because of this flexibility and computational efficiency, `MICE` remains one of the most widely adopted imputation methods in the literature.

Another highly successful approach to imputation has been ensemble methods, such as `HyperImpute`[@hyperimpute] and `RF-GAP`[@rfgap]. `HyperImpute` attempts to make the iterative imputation process more flexible, by allowing a model search using `AutoML`[@automl] methods over multiple regression models for each feature. On the other hand, `RF-GAP` defines a novel proximity measure on an ensemble of binary recursive trees, and computes a proximity-based sum to impute missing values.

## Generative Imputation

Another line of research views imputation as a generative process. The idea is to estimate the conditional distribution of the missing values given the observed ones, and sample from this distribution to impute missing values. Generative models usually sample from a simple, known distribution, like a multivariate normal distribution, and transform these samples to match the required conditional distribution. The mechanism of transformation and the assumed form of the conditional distribution separates these models.

One of the simplest methods to do this is to adapt a \acr{DLVM} to generate imputations for missing values. \acr{DLVM}s draw samples (known as the latent variable) from a simple known prior distribution, usually a Gaussian. They then attempt to approximate the posterior distribution of the observed values over this latent variable by fitting a parameterized family of distributions conditioned on it. This family is usually parameterized as a simple family (like a Gaussian), over a parameterized transformation of the latent variable, usually via a neural network. Sampling from this posterior is often either intractable or has an impractical convergence rate, so amortized variational inference is used to estimate another parameterized proposal distribution that is as close as possible to the posterior. These approaches have been explored in works like @miwae and @notmiwae, for different assumptions on the missingness mechanism.

Another early approach was to modify a \acr{GAN} to generate imputations for missing values. The missing values are initially imputed by draws from a simple distribution like a Gaussian, and then the generator network is used to transform these samples to match the required conditional distribution. An adversarial discriminator network is then trained to estimate the corresponding missingness mask, and then the generator and discriminator are adversarially trained iteratively. This results in imputed that values that the discriminator is unable to discern as imputed.

Due to diffusion models' impressive generative modeling capacity, many imputation approaches based on them have been developed in recent years. One of the first approaches in this direction was \acr{CSDI} models[@csdi], which attempt to impute values at missing time points in multivariate time-series data by conditioning the diffusion model on the observed time points and then denoising from white noise using the conditional diffusion model. Another similar approach[@bridgeImputation] constructs and solves a Schrödinger Bridge problem with conditional constraints to impute missing values in time-series data, where the conditional constraints are derived from the observed values. However, both these approaches are only available for imputation in multivariate time-series data, which is out of the scope of our paper. 

An interesting approach for tabular data[@csdi_t] consists of removing the temporal transformer layers from \acr{CSDI}[@csdi] and constructing embeddings for categorical variables, after which the same diffusion procedure as \acr{CSDI} is applied. Another diffusion-based approach[forestDiffusion] constructs multiple copies of the dataset with different noise samples added, on which gradient-boosted trees are trained to perform the reverse diffusion process to reconstruct the missing data values. The NewImp[@NewImp] model, on the other hand, attempts to learn the missing value distribution by learning the score function of the joint distribution using a Denoising Score Matching approach and then by stepwise reconstructing the missing values using an ODE simulation of the joint distribution based on these learned scores. Another similar approach, MissDiff[@MissDiff], attempts to learn a score-based model by modifying the loss in a conventional Variance Preserving SDE for diffusion models to only consider the observed values.

## Deep Learning Methods for Imputation

Deep learning methods for imputation often involve optimizing for a cleverly constructed loss function that attempts to approximate the imputation error. A major challenge in these approaches is that very often in imputation tasks, the ground truth values are unavailable, and thus cannot be used in the loss function. One simple solution to this is to synthetically mask an additional section of the observed values, and compute the loss using those synthetically masked values as the ground truth.

For instance, a variational autoencoder-based approach[@mae] generates the missing data by training multiple separate variational autoencoders to encode the latent space of each feature and the dependencies among them. This training is helpful in the presence of diverse feature types. `ReMasker`[@remasker] presents a transformer-based encoder-decoder network that attempts to reconstruct the synthetically masked values, using the \acr{MSE} loss. Similarly, `MIRACLE`[@miracle] uses a simple feed-forward neural network to improve naively imputed values. Its loss function is a sum of three terms: a reconstruction term which attempts to reconstruct both the missing values and the missingness mask, and two causal terms which ensure that the inter-variable dependencies form a causal structure as represented by a directed acyclic graph. Another approach based on a modification of OTImputer[@otimputer] attempts to minimize the Wasserstein distance between latent representations of the original and imputed data set generated via a neural network, where the latent representation generating neural network is fit to maximize the Mutual Information to prevent model collapse.

`GRAPE` is a somewhat more novel approach[@grape], which consists of representing the data set as a labeled bipartite graph, with the two node types representing the samples and the features and each edge label representing the value of the particular feature for that sample. One then uses a GraphSAGE[@graphsage] inspired Graph Neural Network to predict the missing edge labels, which are the imputed values.
